newsitem.title: FINLAND: FOCUS-AMER BOUNCES ON OWNERSHIP PLAN.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-AMER BOUNCES ON OWNERSHIP PLAN.

text.p: Shares in Amer Oy, the Finnish sports goods group which owns the Wilson and Atomic golf, tennis and skiing brands, bounced on Tuesday when it revitalised a plan to simplify its complex ownership structure.

In a move greeted by analysts as ending uncertainty and speculation on the company's future, Amer said it would buy back and cancel some of its stock, and propose to shareholders a conversion of vote-heavy K shares into listed A series stock.

The conversion proposal, at one-and-a-half A shares for one K-share, improved on a previous offer in June which domestic institutions vetoed, instead setting a last-minute deal to sell their vote-heavy stakes in the company to a British investor.

"This would mean we have solved a problem that the company has tried to solve for a very long time," Amer CEO Roger Talermo told Reuters. "If we can solve that -- as it looks today -- we will be even stronger to solve the business side."
Amer's stock in Helsinki jumped to 100 markka and later traded at 98.00 markka, up 6.70 or over seven percent, although volume was subdued in a broad lacklustre market.
Amer in January-April made a loss before extraordinaries and taxes of 49 million markka (9 million), against a 114 million loss in the year-ago period.

The plan would end a complex string of deals and broken promises in the past year and a half, since the four domestic institutions who control over 90 percent of votes in the loss-making group said they wanted to sell their stakes.

Amer's situation has been complicated by the fact that the vote-heavy K-stock is unlisted, and Briton Jonathan Bryan Guinness, third Lord Moyne, had offered 273.64 markka per share -- much more than the price of the listed A series.

The shares which Amer bought back and cancelled had been earmarked for sale to Guinness by one of the Finnish institutions, a student group, seeking to cash in fully short-term on the value of its holding.
The other three institutions, who had also agreed to sell to Guinness, later reneged, citing insufficient guarantees.
Talermo said Amer would fund the 75.3 million markka buyback, of shares with about one-tenth of votes, from equity. "Financially it won't make any dent at all, in my opinion," he said.

Talermo said the proposed conversion, on which Amer's K-shareholders will vote at an extra meeting on August 26, stood a better chance of success this time because its three remaining main owners had given a written undertaking to back it.
"We would not try to go this way a second time if we did not think it will work," he said.
Conversion to A-series stock will also boost decision-making rights on Amer's listed series, it said: this would finally bring control of the company into the hands of active investors.
"The A shares will become much more interesting," said Teemu Lahkela at Postipankki. "Earlier the K-shareholders, who have owned just a fraction of the company, have had control of it."

Amer said increased liquidity in its A stock and its clearer ownership structure would also improve its ability to use the A shares to raise equity finance and as a payment for any potential acquisitions.
